utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci. And good morning once more. Same advisory to Defence, accused: Problems with interpretation, please draw our attention straight away. Appearances, I think we are fine. Any preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. I just wanted to point out that today Mr. Ostojic and myself, Mr. Meek, are here for Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You're missing the middle man. Thank you. So we can bring in the witness. Are there people in the gallery or not? So I wish to express our gratitude to the Defence teams for handing in your estimated cross-examination time for the third witness. I appreciate it. In the meantime, we enjoin you to do your utmost to finish with the next witness by the end of this week's sittings. That is Thursday. We are not sitting on Friday. We can make an effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have had Mr. Ruez available, thinking he might get started on Thursday. It may not -- we may not make that, and if it looks like that, we may just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. In fact, I wanted to ask you, is he still working for the Prosecution or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. He's been gone since 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. So in other words, he had to travel here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No problem; it's close by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You looked relaxed. I hope you had a nice, relaxed weekend and that you are ready to proceed with your cross-examination, that you're not feeling too tired for it. And if you cooperate with us by giving simple, short, straightforward answers, I can guarantee you you'll be out of here and on your way back home within an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I also remind you, sir, that you are still testifying under oath, or the solemn declaration that you made when you first started giving evidence here. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, who is next? I think Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Krgovic, sir, is appearing for General Gvero, and he will be putting some questions on cross-examination to you. Mr. Krgovic. The lectern? Are you looking for the lectern? We had a really big one, which is on its way. That's okay. The other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We have a smaller one here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just a few remarks before we start with the cross-examination. Since the two of us speak the same language, I would kindly ask you to make a pause after my question before giving your answer in order to avoid overlapping and in order to contribute towards a clear interpretation. I'm going to try and word questions so that you can answer them simply with a "Yes" or "No" or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you said that you had returned to your village at the beginning of April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The conflicts in that area started sometime towards the end of April the same year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The villagers of your village organised a unit of Territorial Defence in order to defend themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This was the case with other villages in the area as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is how the events followed: You defended, you were attacked, you returned fire, and that's how it went until 1993, until the month of February when you left the village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes we did not return fire. We did not have enough power. We would shift. We would go to another village, a village that had not come under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Initially this was a conflict between the villages, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were first attacked by the unit that had arrived from Zekovici. One Serb arrived and told the villagers that lived on the border of those villages, he said, Brothers - and he started crying - flee! There is the army with tanks in Sekici and Pavlovici and other villages, I don't know what their order is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you here. You've already told us that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I've never told you that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the conflicts in your area. Would you agree that there were -- there was fighting between the villages at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the last thing that happened, a conflict between the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but that was when there was a lot of shelling. People started dying, and then people were forced to leave their villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Krgovic and Witness, you're not allowing a pause between question and answer, and I can already sense the difficulty that the interpreters are having. So please, you particularly Mr. -- Witness, please allow a little bit of a pause. Don't jump straight in with your answer. Mr. Krgovic, sorry for interrupting you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the units in the villages helped each other with equipment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What equipment? What units?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The units of Territorial Defence who helped each other.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know how it was. Only every hundredth person had a rifle. We did not have weapons like you had weapons. The Serbs, I mean. If somebody had means to purchase a weapon, they did. If they didn't have the money, then they might have captured a weapon from the Serbian soldier. We had to help each other because we didn't have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I wanted to ask you. In other words, you helped each other in defending yourselves. Sir, I'll move on to another topic. In your testimony on Thursday, you mentioned an event when, after having been captured, during the night between the 13th and 14th July you were brought to Bratunac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then you mentioned that from the lorry where you were, you heard people approaching the lorries, asking for individuals to stand up if they were from certain villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Since the transcript doesn't clearly show the names of the villages, I'm going to repeat their names and you just say whether that is correct or not, whether these were the villages that you mentioned. Pusmulici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Glogova?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Bljeceva?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Slatina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Those were Muslim villages predominantly, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that in Glogova there were some Orthodox people living but not many. The rest of the villages, I don't know them too well because I hail from a different municipality and this is a different municipality. I know that in Glogova there were a few Orthodox people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the events during that period of time, the conflicts that had broken out in the territory of these villages in the period starting with 1992, finishing in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Pusmulici, Potocari, Slatina, Bljeceva, I wouldn't know. I don't know what happened there, but I know that in Glogova there had been a mass genocide in which 60-something males had been murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. I'm asking you whether you are familiar with the conflicts in those villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about Glogova, that there was a genocide there. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about Kravica, Jezestica, Bjelovac; are you familiar with those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with these villages. I know them well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Ejub Golic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that in June -- I apologise, in August, or 8th of August, 1992, on the 14th and 19th December, 1992, and 7 January, 1993, the units from the villages of Pusmulici, Potocari, Glogova, Bljeceva and Slatina, led by Zulfo Tursunovic and Ejub Golic, had attacked the Serbian villages of Kravice and Jezestica and Bjelovac and completely ruined them and torched them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time I was in my village. That's why I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that these facts -- that the villagers of these villages who participated in these attacks were tried by this Tribunal and sentenced for excessive use of force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened in 1992 because I was in my village. We were separated from each other. Kravica would not communicate with Srebrenica at the time [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could help Mr. Krgovic at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Here in the transcript it's on page 7, line 25, says that Kravica would not communicate with Srebrenica at the time. What I heard from the witness is that Kravica would not let anyone communicate with Srebrenica at the time. This is what he actually said. So perhaps Mr. Krgovic will clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Perhaps you can, if you wish so, to do -- clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand the objection? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody from the free territory, for example, Konjevic Polje, could not communicate with Srebrenica, not with Kravica. Kravica did not communicate with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in the transcript I asked you about a man called Zulfo Tursunovic, and you said you knew him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him as a person, but I never spoke to him and he never spoke to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's go back to the event which happened in Bratunac between the 13th and 14th of July. You said that you had heard that people from these villages had been called. They had been asked for their names and their father's names, and then they would be taken away.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not a roll-call. There was a question, "Is there anybody from that village?" And if somebody says they were, then they would be taken away. There was no roll-call. Nobody knew who was on the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How did you understand why these people were looking for these men? If somebody had told you that this had to do with retaliation for the previous conflict and as a result of the previous conflict that they had been taken away, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't, because their -- genocide had taken place in other places before that. People fell without resistance Zvornik, Bratunac. In the playground in Bratunac more people were killed -- that were killed on -- on the night between the 13th and 14th of July. This was in 1992. All of these genocide that took place in 1992. If this is not part of the indictment, I think it should be. 700-something from people, from Klisa, Djulici [phoen], Bijeli Potok, Sjenokos, and I don't know how many other villages. Lupe. Over 700 people who had surrendered their arms, who had even given the cars of their keys [as interpreted] just to avoid war, all of these people were captured and killed. None of them are still living.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I think you have recovered too much energy, because you are answering giving much more --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no. I'm really doing well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please answer the question and nothing but the question. We don't require more information from you than what you're being asked to answer. I recognised you, Mr. Nicholls, before. What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just going to say that in a way it was the nature of the previous question, which was asking the witness what might have been in the minds of these people and asking him to speculate on a hypothetical that calls, in a way, for a long answer. And I was going to object to that form of the question but I decided not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My question was simple: What was your impression? What was your opinion why these people were taken away? And this is what I wanted from you. How did you construe at that moment? Were these people taken away because somebody wanted to take revenge against them? Is that how you understood the whole situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No further questions. I thank you. Mr. Haynes. Now, Mr. Sarapa will be cross-examining you, and Mr. Sarapa, together with Mr. Haynes, is defending Mr. Pandurevic -- or Colonel Pandurevic, or General Pandurevic. Go ahead, and again, please allow a pause between question and answer, Mr. Sarapa and Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. You said on the 24th of August, before this Trial Chamber, that there were between 15 and 20.000 people who gathered in Susnjari before a column was formed to go to Tuzla. During the night between 11th and 12th, you were in Susnjari. That's where you spent the night. And you also said that all those who were gathered there during that night, that those people spent that night in a meadow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Are we talking about one meadow or several meadows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were big plots of land. There are no small meadows there. And they were connected, these meadows. There was a lot of room. There could have been even more people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately what are -- what is the size of the area where the people were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, if I had known that I would be testifying here, I could have measured. I believe that it was anything between 300 and 500 metres. I never measured it but there was ample room. This was close to the villages, there were no forests there. The meadows were long and wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you see at a glance the entire area where these 15 to 20.000 people were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that night, I could not take in everything at a glance, but in the morning the convoy started moving, and then the groups got smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Your estimate of the number of people, 15 to 20.000 as you told us, is this the result of what you saw, or are there any other elements that helped you to reach that figure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was my pure estimate, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Let me remind you of what you said on the 24th of August here before this Trial Chamber. This is transcript page 24, line -- lines from 1 to 6. As a matter of fact, what is relevant is line -- lines 4 and 5. You said this, and I'm going to translate into B/C/S: "We spoke amongst ourselves. We looked at each other. We thought that there could have been between 15 and 20.000 people." You're talking in plural. Not just you but the others as well. Does that mean that what you heard from the others also made part of the estimate and that your estimate is not based only on what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was smoking with another man. We were observing, and we decided that this was a large group of people. One cannot describe the situation before one sees it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Let's move on. You were at the rear of the column that started moving from Susnjari. That is your testimony. And that part lagged behind during the second night of the journey; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And when the convoy consolidated again - and I'm quoting your words - and as you started moving towards Konjevic Polje, you crossed a forest above Kamenica. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We -- we were still in the forest of Buljim when the Serb forces started calling us to surrender. We arrived at Konjevic Polje by vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yes, I know. This was not the intention and purpose of my question. However, your journey, the journey that you took, took us through the forest above the village of Kamenica. These are your words.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Buljim is that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Very well. Did you pass through the forest above Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't even know what Kamenica is. I only told you that we passed through a torched village, and we knew that this was a Muslim village because it had been torched, and we were supposed to surrender there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Did you see corpses by the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was when we decided to surrender on a slope, and this is where the field started. This was very close to those torched houses. There may have been up to 50 bodies by the road there. There were elderly people, there were also younger people. There was just one person in uniform. His head was covered, I could not see his face, I could not recognise him. As a matter of fact, it's very difficult to recognise anybody who's dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for the witness to be shown his statement that he gave on the 29th of July, 1995, before the court in Tuzla. This is a document in English, and the number is 00795503. This is the ERN number. The last digits are 03, and can we please look at page 5, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just heard somebody's mobile. Please switch off any mobiles, cellular phones that you may have, whoever it is. Apart from the inconvenience, there is also a security issue involved, especially when witnesses -- protected witnesses may be testifying in closed session or in private session. Having mobiles on is not exactly what we should be having. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, I'm sorry to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I just saw the usher putting this statement on the ELMO. I want to make sure we're not broadcasting anything that would identify the witness and some --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I was precisely coming to that but I haven't seen as yet anything on the screen. So let's -- best way to go about it -- is he going to be shown the -- does he have a copy in his own language, to start with? And what you're putting on the ELMO is the English version? All right. So I think we better play it safe and go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: In your statement dated 13 and 14 August, 1995, which you gave to the Investigator Ruez, you said as follows -- about your arrival in Orahovac: "According to the position of the sun, I would say this was early in the afternoon." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Let me just emphasise that this is in the English version page 4, paragraph 6; and in B/C/S this is page 4, paragraph 6 as well. Thank you. On your arrival in Orahovac, you said that there was a ramp or a podium there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I'm just interpreting or trying to quote the words from the transcript as on 24 August of this year, page 70, line 10. The witness spoke about the ramp or the podium, and then he continued in lines 13, 14 and 15 - I'm going to translate into your own language, Witness - I believe that this was not done at the moment when the facility was actually constructed. It may be that this was done a day or two days before, and that is why they had knocked down part of the wall; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, just as a point of -- the way we proceed, I think the transcript should be read by counsel in English and translated in the booths rather than counsel translating the English and reading it to the witness. That way we get sort of official translation. I think that's a better way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I need to consult with my colleagues on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, do you speak any English at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Because the problem may arise when you have counsel that doesn't speak a word of English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour, but then what I understood him to be saying was he was reading the English and translating it himself, which then we have a sort of double translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay, but still it wouldn't solve the problem. In other words, we are prepared to adopt a standard approach to this. However, with the understanding that it doesn't always work, especially when you have co-counsel, counsel who doesn't speak any English. So all right? That's the understanding. Otherwise -- it's okay. I don't think there is a big deal in this part because I think -- I think we're there. There isn't any difference from what was interpreted and what you read or you what you translated yourself. Yes, Mr. Sarapa, you may proceed with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I would like to add something. There is no problem with that. I can read every part of the transcript in English and have the interpreters interpret. I tried to do my interpretation correctly, and if need be, I'll repeat it for the interpreters to correct. Is that necessary or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's a question of the Prosecution asking that at this early stage of the trial we adopt standard practice which will, in other words, be followed in the months to come and the years to come. Yes, Mr. Sarapa. I think he answered your previous question. If you want to put it again, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I would like to follow up with the following question:

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Did you see the remains of the material that came from the knocked down wall; the bricks, the concrete or anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I arrived there in 1999, this was walled up with concrete blocks, and that is how I concluded that this was new. On that day, I had not noticed anything. I had not noticed that there had been any construction going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's now talk about Orahovac. You spoke about the vehicles parked in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how big was the space where these vehicles were parked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. Let me just explain please. The vehicles were not parked. As the vehicles pulled over, the people would get off and then that vehicle would turn around and give room for the others. Not all the vehicles were parked there at all times. When I came there, there was a Centrotrans bus with the registration plate of Serbian Sarajevo, CC, and there was also another bus in front of the building from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can you please define approximately, at least, what was the size of the area in front of the school where the buses could have been parked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a huge area. The courtyard and the area in front of it was huge. When I jumped off the lorry, I ran to the school, and I -- at that moment I couldn't tell how big the area was. I could only see later on how big it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: But you can't tell us about -- anything about the dimension thereof?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You described the sports hall. However, do you remember how many basketball baskets were there in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point I did not see any. I did not pay any attention to that. I did not have the time to see what was on the wall. They wouldn't allow us to look around too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can you please estimate the size of the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To an estimate, it was some 15 metres long, or even -- even longer. I can't be more precise. But when the people measured, I'm sure that they could tell you how long and how wide the sports hall is. In any case, it was a large sports hall. We were sitting with our knees under my -- under our chin. We looked like crouching sculptures. That's how squeezed we were in that sports hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 15 metres or 50 metres, the size of the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was at least 15 metres, that's what I'm saying. But I believe there is a record to that effect. This was measured by somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon. Mr. Sarapa, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yes, I have a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: When you fled Orahovac, what was the weather like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that night the -- the sky was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Sarapa. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I will ask the question again. I apologise. Mr. Nicholls, is there redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. So there are no further questions, neither from the Prosecution nor from the Bench, which basically means that, as I promised you earlier on, your testimony comes -- ends here, comes to an end here, which means that you are free to go. You will now be escorted out of the courtroom by our usher. You will receive all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home at the earliest, and on behalf of my colleagues, Judge Kwon, Judge Prost, and Judge Stole, on behalf of everyone here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I now move to introduce the exhibits which were put in through the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. While we are at this, I would like to raise a matter. I see that the e-court -- person responsible for e-court is here. My attention has been drawn to a possible problem that might arise. Now, Prosecution would be tendering these documents as exhibits and they will be marked accordingly, all right? That's not the problem. But let's suppose that in the course of the cross-examination any of Defence counsel make use of documents that have been entered into the e-court system by the Prosecution and they are -- they wish to make use of them and even tender them as their own, I am told that because of how the system works, they would still carry a P number. So if that is so, I'd like you to do a little bit of brainstorming and assist us, because if they are then also entered into the records as exhibits by the Prosecutor -- Prosecution later on, do we have the same document with the same P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEARCY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but how would we know that it has been tendered by the Prosecution -- by the Defence and not by the Prosecution, or by both, or by just the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEARCY
utterances.text: ... [microphone not activated] which party tendered that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. But it would still carry --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEARCY
utterances.text: It's still ... [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But they can be given a new number as a Court exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but the thing is that, according to them, they can -- if in that case, for example -- in many other -- in many -- in several other cases this happens all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEARCY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it possible that if, for example, Madam Fauveau makes use of one of these Prosecution intended exhibits that are already in the system but not yet tendered as Prosecution exhibits, or already tendered as Prosecution exhibits, and if she wishes to tender the same document as a Defence document, can it be given a D number or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEARCY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It will keep the original number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. What we need to discuss is whether it can be given a D number. This is basically -- because we can always make a copy of it, I understand, and if we can make a hard copy and then it is retendered, it can become a --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEARCY
utterances.text: And then it can become a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we may have found a solution. All right. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEARCY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll now have the next witness, who does not enjoy any protective measures. Correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you see, Mr. Thayer will be leading this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I'm not sure, do I need to remind the usher of the numbers, or are these exhibits already automatically in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the exhibit number follows automatically, as I have understood it, as I have understood the system to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But at least for our own purposes we need to know which are these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This one time, if I can just say them for the record, I believe it was 1691, 1692, 1694, 1697, and P2102 was a marked version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You could follow that, I suppose, Madam Registrar? Madam Registrar, is that all right with you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Out of P numbers, I will keep the P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then we would appreciate if, after the end of the sitting when you send the minutes, et cetera, et cetera, you let us know which is which.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Oric, good morning to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have to check whether Defence is minded to tender those witness statements or not. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Good morning, Mr. President. The Defence would like to tender into evidence one of the statements, the one that I used during my cross-examination, and that was the statement dated 13th and 14th of August. I would like to tender that into evidence with regards to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it will be tendered and kept under seal because of the signature. Other obvious question I need to put to you, Mr. Bourgon, is the following: You did not make use of the entire statement. You only made use of part of the statement. I would just like confirmation from you that it's only that part that was put to the witness that you intend to introduce into the record of the case. In other words, that the understanding amongst us is that the rest will be ignored.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. It was only for -- the part that was used was page -- the bottom of page 8 and the top of page 9 of that statement about the story of a person he met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. But the important thing is that we make this clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The number -- the Defence number was 3D1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 3D1, and I'm sure Madam Registrar can follow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it related to this, Mr. McCloskey? Yes. Go ahead then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I mostly agree with Your Honour on that point, so I won't get to that. The part that they're suggesting into evidence, is it meant for impeachment? Is it meant for substantive evidence? I don't know, given that it -- to help recollect what was said, I have no objection to small parts, but it would be nice to know how the Court considers this. I think under the technical adversarial rules, this kind of material is -- can be meant for impeachment, but as substantive evidence, I don't think so. Though for the purposes of this Tribunal, I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it presents us with any problem, but let's make sure we discuss it and we have a uniform approach to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically the approach is the standard one: That part has been put to the witness, he's answered questions on it, and basically that's -- that's the -- it's only used for us. The rest of the statement we're not interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This -- this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. I am coming to you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with that. Just anticipating, for example, when we have a Prosecution witness that says something that we impeach him with that goes directly to the acts or conduct of the accused, if that is to be looked on as substantive evidence, fine, because are we talking -- if this is substantive evidence, then of course we would like evidence that we use in a similar way as substantive evidence so we know whether to argue it in the brief or not. Is it substantive evidence that can be used or is it mere impeachment that goes to the credibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It -- it can become substantive evidence. Of course it can become -- I mean, the rule is basic. There are various reasons why both of you are allowed to refer a witness to his or her previous out-of-court statement or even previous testimony. And the purposes may vary. If it's for impeachment purposes, then obviously, I mean, you -- you're going to look at it as something substantive. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There shouldn't be any problems on this. Our main interest is to make sure that such previous out-of-court statements, or even previous testimony in this Tribunal or elsewhere, is not introduced as testimony of this witness in this trial unless there is a reason for making use of it, and -- you know the rules, what the rules are. I mean, that's why we -- we pointed this out to Mr. Bourgon, because if his intention was to introduce his -- the previous witness's previous statement as testimony in this case, he got it wrong. I mean, it's not -- I'm not alleging that you tried to do that. But what would come in is the relevant part that he made use of for whatever purpose it was. In this case, it was confronting the witness with part of -- from his previous statement to elicit a clarification from him. But he could have used and you could have used it, as pointed out to us by Judge Kwon, in your re-examination, for example, with the witness. So at that point in time we would -- and if you have any problems as we go along later on, but we will clarify, but these are -- these are the standard -- this is the standard procedure that is relied upon in adversarial systems. Yes, Mr. Haynes. I noticed you before. Sorry for keeping you waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, not at all. Mr. Sarapa put a passage of a witness statement to the last witness. The ERN numbers of that I can give the Court, but in fact it's a released document 7D00001, which is the statement that the last witness made to a court in Tuzla on the 29th of July. The passages that were put to him were put to him for the purpose of contrasting a previous statement that he had made, and as such I suggest and submit that those passages do go into evidence notwithstanding the fact that he disavowed them when they were put to him. The simplest way of doing it is simply to use, as it were, the paragraphs from the Defence released document 7D00001, although it was put to him in hard copy, and the paragraphs were page 6, paragraph 2, in the B/C/S, and page 5, paragraph 2, in the English. And I shall assist the court officer in ensuring that that is achieved before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. The only remaining thing is to see how to go about this in the e-court environment. I wouldn't know how to approach it, but perhaps a copy from hard copy of that paragraph from that statement could be made and then introduced as D7 -- I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you D1?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We're D7 but it's document 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, D7, document number 1. You decide because I just don't want to interfere much with what you have in mind, but the important thing is that we are all then aware of the number, and I thank you so much, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that gives an example, for example, of what the purpose of that extract will be for the purpose of our assessment evaluation of evidence later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Oric, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wish to welcome you to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I do it on behalf of my colleagues in this Trial Chamber. My name is a Carmel Agius, I come from the small island of Malta. I am flanked on my right by Judge Kwon, who comes from South Korea. On my left I have Judge Kimberly Prost from Canada; and on my extreme right Judge Ole Bjorn Stole from Norway, who is a Reserve Judge in this case. Together we are presiding over this trial against the seven accused here. Very soon you will be giving evidence. You've been summoned here to give evidence by the Prosecution, and Madam Usher, who is standing next to you, will be handing to you a piece of paper with a copy of a solemn declaration that you need to make here, which is tantamount to an undertaking, a solemn undertaking on your part that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Please proceed with your solemn undertaking. Then there are a few other things that I need to explain to you and we can start with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. You are now going to be asked questions by Mr. Thayer for the Prosecution. He will then be followed by various lawyers from the various Defence teams assisting the seven accused. Your responsibility and your obligation pursuant to the oath, the solemn undertaking you've taken -- you've made, is to answer all the questions that are put to you truthfully, without any distinction between Prosecution and Defence. One final word of advice to you: If you want to go back home by the time you have anticipated, then I suggest that you limit your answers to what is being asked from you. Don't try to give more information than you are being asked. So if it's a question elicits a simple yes or no, answer, just give a yes or no answer and forget about the rest. When you're asked about the rest, you give that information. Did I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Thayer, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state and spell your name.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: My name is Mevludin Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you please spell your name.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: M-e-v-l-u-d-i-n O-r-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, I would just ask you to move closer to the microphone, if you would, and remind you that before answering the question, whether it's myself, Defence counsel, or Their Honours, please take your time and speak as slowly as you can, because we don't want to miss a word that you've said. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: I was born in the municipality of Srebrenica, in the village of Lehovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you're a Muslim by faith; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, prior to the war breaking out in 1992, did you do various types of work in Bosnia, Serbia, and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly, sir, what types of work did you do in each of those places?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: In Croatia, I worked in construction of houses. In Serbia, I worked in the sugar plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were living in Bosnia, what kind of work did you do, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: I worked in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you also work with your father?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: I did. My father was a construction worker, and we worked together on the construction of houses in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during your time in Croatia, did you come to join the Croatian Ministry of Interior police forces?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And will you just briefly describe for the Trial Chamber, please, how that came about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when it happened precisely. We're talking of pre-1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This took place in February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, how is it that you came to join the Croatian movement?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: They were looking for people to volunteer, the salary was good, so I signed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately how long you served with the Croatian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Not very long. I think 20 days altogether. I left for Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, prior to the war breaking out in 1992, did you perform your mandatory JNA service?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in Gnjilane in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: This was in 1998 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What kind of unit was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Artillery unit. It was in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, by the middle of 1992, had you returned to the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the witness said 1988.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And that would correct what we have in line 10 on page 32; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you please, I can make that clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. We're talking of when he performed the mandatory JNA service, and he would have been 18 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, your mandatory service with the JNA commenced in 1988, not 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, by the middle of 1992, sir, had you returned to the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you have relatives living in that area at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: You mean in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In the Srebrenica area, sir.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of my family lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say you had a number of relatives living in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Many of them lived there. Two families; family Oric and my mother's family, Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was one of your relatives Naser Oric, the former commander of the 28th Division of the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is my cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, after you returned to the Srebrenica area in 1992, did Naser Oric ask you to make a trip to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did, to go fetch a doctor and to get some medicines and other supplies. I didn't go by myself. I was accompanied by other mates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, let's please be specific as to the time when this happened, because the previous indication is that somewhere around about the middle of 1992 you returned to Srebrenica area but we don't know when this request by Naser Oric was made to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you recall, sir, approximately when you made this trip to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Sometime in July, end of July. I don't recall the exact day, but end of July, 1992. This is when I came back to Srebrenica, and after ten days I went back to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At first, sir, did you want to make this trip to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. When I went to Srebrenica, I realised how dangerous it was. We went through minefields, and I didn't want to go back. When Naser told me to go to the hospital and see what was happening there, he told me to make up my own mind. When I came to the hospital, I saw the hospital was full of -- of people. There were no bandages, that they had to sever people's legs, and I decided to -- to start for this journey when I saw this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I hate to interrupt my colleague during his examination-in-chief, but we have been provided in the pre-trial brief for the Prosecution with a summary that tells us what this witness is supposed to testify about. Now, I notice from this summary that there is nothing about this trip to Tuzla in 1992. I don't know what the relevance of it is, and since the beginning, even though my colleague has been leading the witness, we don't object because it's very benign information, but now we're talking about a trip, and we're talking about Naser Oric, and we're talking about 1992. Maybe my colleague can establish the basis for asking these questions, because they're outside of this summary. And there was recently, Mr. President, in the case of the Prosecutor versus Milutinovic, a decision rendered by the Trial Chamber in that case saying that it is absolutely critical for the Prosecution to remain within the confines of the summary that they provided the Defence with. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Your Honour, the relevance of this line of questioning will, I believe, be clear within a few moments. I just have one or two more questions on this issue. The information contained in these questions and in the responses was present in his statements which have been disclosed to the Defence. Granted, the summary which we provided did not include every single piece of information that we intended to elicit from this witness, but it is information that has been disclosed. I have just one or two more questions, I believe the relevance will become clear, and then I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So was this part covered or included in the previous testimony of this witness in Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This information was, Your Honour. Specifically on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. I see you standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not saying that this information was not part of the material that was given to the Defence, I'm just saying that this is the procedure that we use in the sense that when we have a summary that is provided by the Prosecutor, they have to keep to that summary. When there are changes, they give us proofing notes further to their meeting with the witness. In this case, we have been provided with proofing notes and this topic was not raised in the proofing notes. Now, I have the decision here from the Trial Chamber in the Milutinovic case, which is an oral decision, which I can help the Trial Chamber with, if necessary. But I'd like that if we could stick to the fact that if we have a summary, then that the Prosecution maintains the evidence with what was in the summary. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that. I don't think that there is a need for a decision from us on this given the circumstances, but I suggest that you take this up between you after the sitting and agree that this will be so in the future, and that it is, of course, more than desirable that you each stick to what is contained in the summary, because otherwise there -- there -- that would -- departure from that would mean surprises and loss of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, sir, what route did you follow to get from the Srebrenica area to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: I went through Konjevic Polje, Carska, Kamenica, through the forest, through the hills. Snagovo to Tuzla. Mainly through the forest, through the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions now about your military service briefly, sir. Between 1992 and 1995 and the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, is it fair to say that you were a soldier with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is it also fair to say that you became a commander of a squad near your village in Lehovici?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a commander of a squad which is not from Polici [phoen] but from the surrounding villages, all the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And typically speaking, sir, can you describe what the nature of your military activity was with this squad during that period of time, just generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Our duty was to guard our lines, the lines that we maintained on the -- on the hill of Burije. That was our task. Our task was to defend the villages of Susnjari, Jaglovici, Brazoveneva [phoen], Babuljica, Lehovici, Gorsovici [phoen] and so on. This was our task. It was defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, by July of 1995, sir, did your squad have any arms?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: We had a rifle, one rifle. A semi-automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where was that rifle kept, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Whatever rifles there were, they were on the lines, and as the shifts changed, they would take over the previous shift's arms. We -- we did not all have arms, and we couldn't take arms home. Whatever arms we had were on the line. So the rifles would stay on the line all the time. People would go home, but they wouldn't take weapons with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've concluded this section. I understand we have a break coming up in a couple of minutes. If this is a good time for the Court, I can break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We will have a short break now, 20 minutes. Twenty minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like now to turn your attention to the first week to 10 days of July, 1995, just prior to the fall of Srebrenica. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: At the time, I resided in the village of Lehovici, near Srebrenica. And during those 10 days, one morning I woke up in Srebrenica in my sister's house. She resided in Srebrenica at the time. When I got up, I heard shots and shelling, the shelling of Srebrenica. This was the beginning of the attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: In the village of Lehovici. During the time when Srebrenica was attacked, I was in Lehovici, near Srebrenica. That's where I was born as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with whom were you living at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: With my father, mother, my wife, and my two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you stated that your sister resided in Srebrenica at the time, and that you experienced part of the attack. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber, during the attack on Srebrenica during this period of time, what you observed personally with your eyes or ears.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Well, in the morning when I woke up, I heard shelling. I went out of the apartment, I asked passers-by what was going on. They said nobody knew anything. Everybody was surprised by the shelling. We knew that this was a protected area, that there should be no shooting. And I was also surprised. I realised that this was a real attack, real shelling, and I headed back towards my house in Lehovici immediately. Shells were falling all over the place, all sorts of calibre. I immediately headed towards my house. I thought that I would be necessary in my unit for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what were the targets of the shelling? What were the shells striking, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: In the town of Srebrenica, it was populated by civilians. The town was full of civilians, of citizens. So the targets was everything that was moving. Everything was targeted. They did not target anything in particular. Everything was targeted; houses, buildings. Wherever shells could fall, they fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you estimate for the Court, sir, approximately how many days the shelling lasted.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I believe for seven days, day and night, the shelling never stopped. The shelling of the town itself, I mean. Where I lived in Lehovici there was no shelling. No shells fell there. The main targets were Srebrenica and Donji Potocari. My village was not hit by any shells. Srebrenica was the target, and it was shelled seven days, day in and day out, day and night, without stopping. I'm not sure about the number of days, but approximately, I would say, that the shelling lasted for seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recall learning on 11 July that the town of Srebrenica had actually fallen?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: When I learned that Srebrenica had fallen, I was on a line, the line on Jaglici close to the UNPROFOR base. The UNPROFOR troops had fled, and we had to look after the line in their stead. I was there all day, and I didn't know anything. It was only in the evening, around 6.00 or half past 6.00 that I went to the village of Jaglici to see what was going on. As I arrived in the village, there was nobody there. I just bumped into a woman, I asked her what was going on, and then she told me through tears that Srebrenica had fallen and that all the people went in the direction of UNPROFOR's base in Potocari. I returned, and I told my fellow fighters what had happened, that we had to withdraw and that we should wait and see what would happen, that we just had to stay put. From there, we started towards the village of Susnjari. I arrived at my sister's house. I was with her. She was also crying and packing her belongings. I told her to stay calm because whatever would happen would happen. From there, I went to my own house to see what was going on with my family. I bumped into my neighbour on the way there and they told me not to go there because on that very day shells started falling on my village as well and that my family is in Potocari and that there was no need for me to go home. I returned with these neighbours to the house in Susnjari, to Sead's house. This is where people started gathering, and the command from Srebrenica arrived there as well, and this is where we were. This is where I stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall approximately what time of day you arrived in Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: This was in the evening, around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why was Susnjari selected as a gathering location, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: This was surrounded by hills, in a valley. Thus it was best protected from any shelling or observation. Nobody could observe that area from the hilltops. They could not see us gathering there, and they could not target us there. We were well-protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you stated a moment ago that the command from Srebrenica also arrived at Susnjari. Was there a decision that was made at some point regarding what was going to happen next?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: How shall I put it? We discussed as to what should be done, where we should go, whether to go towards Zepa or Tuzla. And sometime in the evening, around 10.00 maybe, or even later, I don't know, I did not look at the watch, a decision was made to head towards Tuzla. The de-mining units immediately set off towards Tuzla to clear the terrain from landmines, and after them the other units started walking single file after them, and that's -- that's what went on for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let me back up a moment, sir, and just ask you a couple of specific questions about the gathering at Susnjari. When you arrived there, approximately how many military-aged men would you estimate were there with you already?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: There was a total of maybe 15.000 men, children. There were quite a few women who went with us. I can't say that they were all of military age. I don't -- I only know that there was a total of some 15.000 people, ranging in age between 14 and 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you right there, sir. I just want to clarify for the record, and I think you've done so, but just to make sure. It's 15.000 persons were gathered there, military-aged men, some -- some women and children as well; is that correct? Not 50.000, 15.000?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Fifteen thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at Susnjari, were there 15.000 people already or did people arrive during the period of time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: People were coming from all sides while I was there. They came from Suceska, in the villages around Suceska, from Srebrenica, from Gornji Potocari, Donji Potocari, and most of them came from the town of Srebrenica itself, which was the most densely populated area. In other words, they kept on coming while I was already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did any of your relatives also join you at Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: As far as my relatives are concerned, all the men from Lehovici joined us. My father joined me as well as my brother-in-law and my nephew, who was 14. His name is Mirza. I told him that he shouldn't be with us, that he should go to Potocari. There were also some neighbours of ours. My uncle's son, who is also 14, and I told him to go to Susnjari because the other terrain was dangerous. I had passed through there in a few years before. There was my neighbour Alija with her brother. I told them as well that it was dangerous, that they should go to Potocari, but they decided against that. They wanted to stay with us. That's how they set off with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that the decision was made for those people to set off towards Tuzla. You weren't sure exactly what time the decision was made or what time they departed, but can you describe for the Trial Chamber, please, in what kind of formation this group was organised.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, it was first the de-mining unit and the troops that were armed. They were ahead of the column. And then the column was organised in brigades. One brigade followed the other. And that's how we set out. That's how we started leaving the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was the entire column armed or were certain sections of the column armed, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Only in parts of the column. There were some men in the brigades that carried arms. Every brigade had a few men carrying arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to arms, sir, you're referring to military weapons as opposed to, say, hunting weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Well, as for the hunting weapons, there were quite a few of those because people had those from before the war. Those who had hunted before the war carried those arms. And there were also other types of weapons, other types of more serious weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was there a proposed route that the column that was going to try to follow, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Well, the column headed towards Konjevic Polje, towards Cerska, Kamenica, all the way up to Tuzla. That was the only route that we had in mind, and that's the route that we followed. That's what we set out to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's roughly the same route, sir, that you followed on your trip to Tuzla that you described earlier in your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, this may sound like an obvious question, but were the men, women, and children in this column Muslim or were they some other faith, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: All Muslim. There was a Serb lady who resided in Srebrenica who had stayed with us and lived with us there, and she was with us. I'm sure that she was there with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you described the de-mining unit leading the column on this route. Did the rest of the column follow right away or did it leave in sections or parts, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: The column followed the de-miners. The de-miners were in the front of the column and the column followed. As they advanced, the column advanced after them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time of day you left Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: The de-miners set out during the night, and the column followed. Throughout the night people were leaving, and I believe that I left sometime in the morning. I don't know how late it may have been, but it was already a day. Maybe around 9.00. I -- I was amongst the last. Not the last but amongst the last of those who left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this would have been the morning of 12 July; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, were you armed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had two grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what were you -- what kind of clothes were you wearing, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall with any more detail what types of clothes you were wearing? What did you have on?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: A pair of jeans, a shirt, a jacket. Simple civilian clothes, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as your part of the column travelled during the course of the day on the 12th of July, was it attacked?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: As we were leaving in the morning, we were fired from the place called Jezestica, and they ordered us to hurry up, and they cursed us. At one moment, the column was interrupted, and as soon as the shooting started, we continued on the same road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that you spent most of the day on 12 July following the column on this path?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I left Jaglici, I saw the first victims in the first stream. There were six of them who fell victim to a mortar shell. They fell on the spot. Their bodies were shattered. And those were the first victims that I saw as I was leaving Jaglici and as I was moving towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you right there, sir. Is it fair to say that on your trek during the course of that day you saw numerous bodies of people that had been killed or wounded along -- along the path?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw in another place two bodies, and then in a third place some more. There were ambushes all the way, and every 50 metres or so I saw bodies. We were under constant fire. We bumped into numerous ambushes, and that's what I could observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, towards the night-time on 12 July, did your portion of the column reach a particular village where you were ambushed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes. We arrived sometime in the evening at the village of Kamenica in Bratunac municipality. As we arrived there, there had been a previous agreement that we should stop there and rest. The first half of the column was already on the way to Tuzla, but the other half decided to take a rest there at that place. We sat down to rest, and after a certain while shooting started at the spot. There was shelling, there were rifle bursts. And when the shooting stopped, when everything was over, I believe that over a hundred people had been killed in that place. There were a lot of injured. A lot of people fled towards Siljkovici and Kravica, straight into the arms of the Chetniks who waited for them in Kravica and Sekovici because they were not familiar with the terrain, with the route. I believe that at least 500 people fell victim as a result of that. They were all either killed on the spot or injured or went missing after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I am beginning to think that at this point, since more or less I am the only one who is pretty much familiar with the area, that in order to be able to understand properly, we need to have pretty much a detailed map area. But in other words, Susnjari, Jaglici, Jezestica, that has been -- and now Kamenica. And perhaps the witness can also explain to us when he means, "We arrived sometime in the evening at the village of Kamenica in Bratunac." Does he mean to say that they entered the village of Kamenica? Because to my knowledge, Kamenica was Serb controlled at that time. So perhaps he can --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we do certainly need a map so we can follow at least the route taken by the convoy in the -- in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. It was my intention not to show him a map and leave that to a subsequent witness. However, I can certainly, at the next break, arrange to have him shown, I think probably map 5, if I recall, in the map book. It may be the best map to do that with and trace the route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what I mean, it will be better for us if we have a survey map, a proper survey map, which would indicate to us at least the route taken. I know that you use the word route in the States, but whether they were following the river, whether they were following the hills and the mountains, whether they were following -- whichever way, because we're talking of Jezestica, which is in the vicinity of Kravica, and this is a main Serbian stronghold at the time. So I think it will give us a much clearer picture of where they were heading or which route they were taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can certainly do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At your pleasure I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time. Perhaps one of your staff can start looking into that. When I said so, I didn't mean I want it now. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just to assist my colleague, here in the transcript we have on page 46, line 20, it says Kravica and Sekovici, and I don't believe that's what witness said.
